questions.q: How do ADK workflow agents (SequentialAgent, ParallelAgent, LoopAgent) orchestrate their sub-agents?
options: Using predefined deterministic logic without consulting an AI model to orchestrate (while sub-agents can still be LLM agents and call tools)
By calling an LLM router before every step to decide which sub-agent runs next
By prohibiting sub-agents from using an LLM or calling any tools
By converting all sub-agents into static SQL queries
questions.yours: By calling an LLM router before every step to decide which sub-agent runs next
questions.correct: Using predefined deterministic logic without consulting an AI model to orchestrate (while sub-agents can still be LLM agents and call tools)
questions.why: Workflow agents (SequentialAgent, ParallelAgent, LoopAgent) run sub-agents using fixed, predefined logic without paying a model call to route. Their sub-agents can still be LLM agents and call tools.

questions.q: In an ADK 2.0 graph, what is the difference between setting data on an Event's 'state' field versus using 'output'?
options: Setting an Event's 'state' field lets any downstream node read it, whereas 'output' passes data only to the immediate next node
'output' is readable by all downstream nodes, whereas 'state' only reaches the immediate next node
Both 'state' and 'output' pass data only to the immediate next node
Neither 'state' nor 'output' can pass data between graph nodes
questions.yours: 'output' is readable by all downstream nodes, whereas 'state' only reaches the immediate next node
questions.correct: Setting an Event's 'state' field lets any downstream node read it, whereas 'output' passes data only to the immediate next node
questions.why: Nodes set shared state through an Event's 'state' field so any downstream node can read it. In contrast, 'output' passes data only to the immediate next node.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a real ADK SessionService implementation (a classic exam distractor)?
options: TextEmbeddingService
InMemorySessionService
DatabaseSessionService
VertexAiSessionService
questions.why: The three real SessionService implementations are InMemorySessionService, DatabaseSessionService, and VertexAiSessionService. 'TextEmbeddingService' is a made-up distractor to watch out for.

questions.q: In ADK's before_tool_callback, what happens when the callback returns None versus returning a dict?
options: Returning None allows normal tool execution; returning a dict blocks/short-circuits the tool and returns that dict to the LLM
Returning None blocks the tool call; returning a dict allows normal execution
Returning a dict deletes the current session state
Both None and dict skip the tool call and terminate the agent
questions.yours: Returning None blocks the tool call; returning a dict allows normal execution
questions.correct: Returning None allows normal tool execution; returning a dict blocks/short-circuits the tool and returns that dict to the LLM
questions.why: In before_tool_callback, returning None allows the tool to execute normally, whereas returning a dict blocks/short-circuits the tool execution and returns that dict directly to the LLM.

questions.q: [Q-M2-23] A CE is building an inventory of a customer's agentic components. Which one will NOT show up in the Agent Registry unless someone manually creates a Service resource for it?
options: An ADK A2A agent deployed to Cloud Run
An agent deployed on Agent Runtime (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform)
A GKE deployment that carries the Agent Registry annotations
An official Google Cloud remote MCP server
questions.yours: An official Google Cloud remote MCP server
questions.correct: An ADK A2A agent deployed to Cloud Run
questions.why: Auto-registration covers: (1) Agent Runtime (GEAP), (2) Google Workspace built-in agents/extensions, (3) Gemini Enterprise (Discovery Engine), (4) GKE deployments with Agent Registry annotations, and (5) official Google/Google Cloud remote MCP servers. Cloud Run deployments are NOT auto-discovered; they require manual registration via the writable Service resource (gcloud agent-registry services create).

questions.q: A team deploys agents across Google Cloud. Which deployment requires MANUAL registration in Agent Registry?
options: An agent deployed on Cloud Run
An agent deployed on Agent Runtime (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform)
A GKE deployment with Agent Registry annotations
An official Google Cloud remote MCP server
questions.yours: An official Google Cloud remote MCP server
questions.correct: An agent deployed on Cloud Run
questions.why: Agent Runtime, annotated GKE, Gemini Enterprise, Workspace agents, and official Google MCP servers auto-register once the API is enabled. Cloud Run is NOT auto-discovered and must be registered manually.

questions.q: [Q-M2-26] Which statement about Agent Registry concepts is NOT accurate?
options: Endpoints are deterministic functions served by MCP servers. Registering them is how you govern which tools an agent can invoke.
A Binding is a connection between a source agent and a target resource: an agent, an MCP server, or an endpoint.
A Skill Revision is an immutable, versioned snapshot, so you can update a skill's instructions or code without changing the parent skill's identifier.
An A2A Skill is declarative capability metadata inside an Agent Card. A standalone Skill is an executable package registered as a top-level resource.
questions.yours: A Skill Revision is an immutable, versioned snapshot, so you can update a skill's instructions or code without changing the parent skill's identifier.
questions.correct: Endpoints are deterministic functions served by MCP servers. Registering them is how you govern which tools an agent can invoke.
questions.why: Tools (not Endpoints) are the deterministic functions served by MCP servers. Endpoints represent target URLs (typically legacy REST APIs); registering them is how you centrally govern and audit which external APIs your agents are allowed to communicate with.

questions.q: A security engineer wants to grant an agent IAM permission to query BigQuery. Should they use the Agent Identifier or the Agent Principal?
options: Agent Principal (principal://...), because Agent Identifier (urn:agent:...) is only for catalog lookup and never used in IAM
Agent Identifier (urn:agent:...), because it is the primary IAM identity for all agents
Either one, because Identifier and Principal are interchangeable in IAM bindings
Neither, because agents can never hold an IAM identity for Google Cloud resources
questions.yours: Neither, because agents can never hold an IAM identity for Google Cloud resources
questions.correct: Agent Principal (principal://...), because Agent Identifier (urn:agent:...) is only for catalog lookup and never used in IAM
questions.why: Identifier (urn:agent:...) is a logical catalog name used only for inventory and lookup—never in IAM. Principal (principal://...) is the SPIFFE/service-account IAM identity used for permissions and auditing.

questions.q: [Section 1.4 • Identifier vs. Principal] A security architect tries to grant BigQuery read permissions in an IAM policy binding using an agent's 'urn:agent:...' string from Agent Registry, and the binding is rejected. Why?
options: 'urn:agent:...' is the logical Agent Identifier used only for catalog inventory and lookup (not used in IAM bindings); IAM permissions and auditing require the Agent Principal ('principal://...', backed by SPIFFE/service account).
'urn:agent:...' only works in IAM Deny policies, whereas IAM Allow policies require an OAuth 2.0 client ID.
The Agent Identifier must first be registered in Discovery Engine before IAM can evaluate it.
Agents cannot use IAM principals for Google Cloud resources and must always use 3-legged user-delegated OAuth.
questions.yours: Agents cannot use IAM principals for Google Cloud resources and must always use 3-legged user-delegated OAuth.
questions.correct: 'urn:agent:...' is the logical Agent Identifier used only for catalog inventory and lookup (not used in IAM bindings); IAM permissions and auditing require the Agent Principal ('principal://...', backed by SPIFFE/service account).
questions.why: Per Core Guide §1.4: 'Identifier' (urn:agent:...) is a logical catalog identifier used for inventory and lookup—it is NEVER used in IAM bindings. 'Principal' (principal://...) is the SPIFFE/service-account-backed IAM identity used for permissions and auditing.

questions.q: What is the correct four-stage operating sequence in Agent Registry?
options: Register → Discover → Govern → Orchestrate
Discover → Register → Orchestrate → Govern
Govern → Register → Discover → Orchestrate
Register → Orchestrate → Discover → Govern
questions.why: The four stages are Register → Discover → Govern → Orchestrate. You Govern (configure access and bindings) right before ADK Orchestrates the resolved endpoints and tools.

questions.q: In Agent Registry, what is the difference between a Tool and an Endpoint?
options: Tools are deterministic functions served by MCP servers; Endpoints are target URLs (like legacy REST APIs) governed in the registry
Endpoints are deterministic functions on MCP servers; Tools are legacy REST URLs
Tools and Endpoints are two names for the exact same MCP resource
Endpoints are only for Gemini Enterprise, while Tools are only for Cloud Run
questions.yours: Endpoints are deterministic functions on MCP servers; Tools are legacy REST URLs
questions.correct: Tools are deterministic functions served by MCP servers; Endpoints are target URLs (like legacy REST APIs) governed in the registry
questions.why: Watch out for the swapped-definition trap: Tools are deterministic functions served by MCP servers, whereas Endpoints represent target URLs (typically REST APIs) registered for governance.

questions.q: A developer wants a custom skill to be available globally across all projects in Antigravity, the IDE, and the CLI. Where should they place it?
options: ~/.gemini/config/skills/
<project-root>/.agents/skills/
~/.config/gcloud/skills/
/usr/local/share/adk/skills/
questions.why: Global skills live in ~/.gemini/config/skills/ and work across Antigravity, the IDE, and the CLI.

questions.q: In a skill's required SKILL.md YAML frontmatter, which field is REQUIRED and which is OPTIONAL?
options: description is required; name is optional
name is required; description is optional
Both name and version are required; description is optional
No YAML frontmatter is used in SKILL.md
questions.yours: name is required; description is optional
questions.correct: description is required; name is optional
questions.why: In SKILL.md's YAML frontmatter, 'description' is required (because the agent uses it to decide when the skill is relevant), while 'name' is optional.
